front: Order the binding times from earliest to latest.
back: Language design → language implementation → compile → link → load → run. Earlier binding gives efficiency, later gives flexibility.

front: Which compiler phase catches a type mismatch?
back: Semantic analysis. A missing semicolon is syntax; an illegal character is lexical.

front: Name the six phases of a compiler.
back: Lexical analysis, syntax analysis, semantic analysis, intermediate code generation, code optimisation, code generation. The symbol table and error handler span all six.

front: Does EBNF describe more languages than BNF?
back: No. Its braces and brackets are shorthand for recursion and alternation; both describe exactly the context-free languages.

front: How is operator associativity encoded in a grammar?
back: By the side of the recursion. Left recursion ⇒ left associativity; right recursion ⇒ right associativity.
Row major: $\text{base} + [(i-l_1)n_2 + (j-l_2)]w$, multiplying by the number of **columns**. Column major multiplies by the number of **rows** instead.
Name equivalence needs the same declared name; structural equivalence needs the same construction. Name equivalence is the stricter rule.
An expression designating a storage location that can be assigned to. In C an array name has an r-value but no l-value, so `a = b;` is illegal for arrays.
Coercion is an implicit conversion inserted by the compiler; a cast is written explicitly by the programmer. Every coercion rule weakens type checking.

front: What do the two meanings of `static` do in C?
back: On a local variable it extends the lifetime to the whole program (initialised once, default 0). On a global or function it restricts linkage to the current file.

front: What is `a[i]` equivalent to in C?
back: `*(a + i)` — and therefore also `i[a]`, which is legal C. Pointer arithmetic is scaled by `sizeof(*a)`.
The array is 3 writable bytes and `sizeof` gives 3. The pointer points at a read-only literal, `sizeof` gives the pointer size, and modifying the literal is undefined.

front: sizeof a struct versus a union?
back: Struct = sum of members plus padding, rounded to the largest alignment. Union = size of the largest member.

front: What does short-circuit evaluation mean for side effects?
back: In `a && b`, if `a` is false then `b` — including any increment inside it — never executes. Same for `a || b` when `a` is true.
The program name plus all arguments. `./prog x y` gives `argc == 3`, with `argv[0]` the program name and `argv[argc]` NULL.
`#define SQR(x) x*x` expands `SQR(1+1)` to `1+1*1+1` = 3, not 4. Writing `((x)*(x))` fixes it. Macros substitute text, not values.

front: Order of construction and destruction in C++?
back: Construction: base class, then member objects in **declaration** order, then the derived constructor body. Destruction is exactly the reverse.

front: Why must a copy constructor take a reference?
back: Passing by value would need a copy, which invokes the copy constructor, which needs a copy — infinite recursion. The compiler rejects `T(T)`.
Overloading: same scope, different signatures, resolved at compile time. Overriding: base and derived, identical signature, resolved at run time if virtual.

front: Which operators cannot be overloaded in C++?
back: `.` `.*` `::` `?:` and `sizeof`. Everything else can be.
A per-class table of virtual function pointers. Each polymorphic object carries a hidden `vptr` to it, so a virtual call costs one extra indirection and resolves by the object's dynamic type.

front: What is the diamond problem and its fix?
back: With `D` inheriting from `B` and `C` which both inherit `A`, `D` holds two copies of `A` and member access is ambiguous. Virtual inheritance (`class B : virtual public A`) collapses it to one shared sub-object.

front: Why should a base class destructor be virtual?
back: Otherwise `delete basePtr;` on a derived object destroys only the base part — undefined behaviour and a leak.

front: Access through public, protected and private inheritance?
back: Public keeps public/protected as they are; protected demotes public to protected; private demotes everything to private. Base private members are never accessible either way.
Well-formed obeys XML syntax (one root, all tags closed and nested, attributes quoted). Valid is well-formed **and** conforms to a DTD or schema. Valid implies well-formed, never the reverse.
DTD has its own syntax, no data types and no namespace support. XSD is written in XML, has rich data types, namespaces and `minOccurs`/`maxOccurs` cardinality.
DOM builds the whole tree in memory: random access, high memory. SAX is event-driven and streaming: low memory, forward-only, no random access.
`init()` → `start()` → `paint()` → `stop()` → `destroy()`. `init` and `destroy` run once; `start`/`stop` run on every page visit and departure. No `main()`.
`init()` once, `service()` once per request (dispatching to `doGet`/`doPost`), `destroy()` once. One instance, a new thread per request — so instance variables are shared.
GET puts data in the URL: visible, length-limited, cacheable, bookmarkable, idempotent. POST puts it in the body: hidden, unlimited, not cached, not idempotent.
Raster draws every pixel from a frame buffer — good for shaded images, shows jaggies. Random (vector) scan draws only the lines from a display list — smooth lines, used for CAD.
width × height × ⌈log₂(colours)⌉ bits. 1024×768 with 256 colours = 1024×768×8 bits = 768 KB.
Line: $p_0 = 2\Delta y - \Delta x$. Midpoint circle: $p_0 = 1 - r$. Both use integer arithmetic only.
DDA uses floating-point increments and accumulates rounding error. Bresenham uses integer decision parameters — faster and exact.
A circle has 8-way symmetry so only one octant is computed. An ellipse has only 4-way symmetry and needs two regions, split where the slope reaches −1.
Boundary fill recurses until it meets a specified **boundary** colour. Flood fill replaces a specified **interior** colour. Both come in 4- and 8-connected forms.
They turn translation into a matrix multiplication, so any chain of transformations collapses into a single matrix product.

front: How do you rotate about an arbitrary point?
back: $T(p)\cdot R(\theta)\cdot T(-p)$ — translate the pivot to the origin, rotate, translate back. The same sandwich works for scaling and reflection about any fixed point or line.
$s_x = \dfrac{xv_{max}-xv_{min}}{xw_{max}-xw_{min}}$ and similarly for $s_y$. If $s_x \ne s_y$ the image is distorted.
Trivially accept if OR of the two codes is 0000; trivially reject if AND is non-zero; otherwise clip against one boundary at a time.
Sutherland–Hodgman, boundary by boundary. Weiler–Atherton is needed for concave polygons, which Sutherland–Hodgman can leave with spurious edges.
$n$, where there are $n+1$ control points. Four control points give a cubic. The curve passes through only the first and last control points.
B-splines give local control, allow the degree to be chosen independently of the control point count, and give $C^{d-2}$ continuity automatically. Bezier has none of these.
Diffuse $I = k_dI_l(N\cdot L)$ is independent of the viewer. Specular $I = k_sI_l(R\cdot V)^{n_s}$ depends on the viewer; larger $n_s$ gives a tighter highlight.
Gouraud interpolates **intensities** computed at vertices — misses highlights inside a facet. Phong interpolates **normals** and lights per pixel — slower but correct.
Parallel keeps proportions measurable (engineering drawings); perspective foreshortens with distance for realism and has one, two or three vanishing points.
